content: Nitroglycerin is prescribed to prevent chest pain, also known as angina. It achieves this by relaxing the blood vessels in the heart, which increases blood flow and oxygen supply to the heart. This medication may also be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Nitroglycerin is available in various forms, including sublingual tablets, buccal tablets, extended-release capsules, and sprays for oral use. Buccal extended-release tablets and extended-release capsules are typically taken three to six times daily. Do not crush, chew, or divide extended-release tablets or capsules. Buccal extended-release tablets can also be used during an angina attack or just before activities known to provoke attacks, such as physical exertion or exposure to cold weather. Always follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take nitroglycerin exactly as directed, without altering the dose or frequency unless instructed by your doctor. Nitroglycerin helps control chest pain but does not cure it. Continue using the medication even if you feel well, and do not stop taking it without consulting your doctor, as abrupt discontinuation may cause chest pain. Prolonged use of nitroglycerin can lead to tolerance, reducing its effectiveness. If your angina attacks become more frequent, last longer, or are more severe, contact your doctor immediately. For buccal extended-release tablets, place the tablet between your cheek and gum and allow it to dissolve without chewing or swallowing it. If you feel dizzy, sit down after placing the tablet in your mouth. Avoid swallowing saliva until the tablet has dissolved. These tablets typically start working within 2–3 minutes. To speed up dissolution, you can touch the tablet with your tongue before placing it in your mouth or drink a hot liquid. If an attack occurs while a buccal tablet is in place, place a second tablet on the opposite side of your mouth. If chest pain persists, use sublingual tablets, call for emergency assistance, or go to a hospital emergency department immediately. If you are using sublingual tablets or spray for acute chest pain, always carry them with you. Sit down when an acute attack occurs. The medication begins to work within 2 minutes and lasts up to 30 minutes. If chest pain is not relieved within 5 minutes after taking a sublingual tablet, take another dose. If using the spray, repeat the process if pain persists after 3–5 minutes. Seek emergency assistance if pain continues after three doses of tablets (at 5-minute intervals) or three sprays (at 3–5-minute intervals) and 15 minutes have passed. To use sublingual tablets, place one under your tongue or between your cheek and gum and allow it to dissolve. Avoid swallowing the tablet or saliva too often until it has dissolved. To use the spray, hold the container upright without shaking it. Position the spray mechanism close to your open mouth, press the mechanism with your forefinger to release the spray onto or under your tongue, and close your mouth immediately. Do not inhale or swallow the spray. Nitroglycerin tablets may also be used in combination with other medications to treat congestive heart failure and heart attacks. Discuss the potential risks of using this medication for your condition with your doctor. Before taking nitroglycerin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to nitroglycerin, isosorbide (e.g., Imdur, Isordil, Sorbitrate), or any other drugs. Notify your doctor if you have anemia, glaucoma, or a history of recent head trauma. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking nitroglycerin, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform your healthcare provider that you are taking nitroglycerin. Be aware that this medication may cause drowsiness or dizziness; avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how it affects you. Consult your doctor about the safe use of alcohol while taking nitroglycerin, as alcohol can exacerbate its side effects. Take nitroglycerin extended-release tablets and capsules on an empty stomach with a full glass of water. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Common side effects of nitroglycerin include headache, rash, dizziness, upset stomach, and flushing (a sensation of warmth). If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects, such as blurred vision, dry mouth, chest pain, or fainting, require immediate medical attention. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store nitroglycerin in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Do not puncture the spray container, and keep it away from heat. Do not open a container of sublingual nitroglycerin until you need a dose. Discard tablets that are more than 12 months old. Dispose of outdated or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the victim has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Nitroglycerin extended-release capsules should not be used for acute angina attacks. Continue using nitroglycerin tablets or spray to relieve chest pain that has already started. If headaches persist, consult your doctor about taking acetaminophen. Do not take aspirin or other headache medications while on nitroglycerin unless directed by your doctor. The tablets may cause a sweet, tingling sensation when placed under the tongue, but the absence of this sensation does not indicate reduced drug effectiveness. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist with any questions about refilling your prescription.
